My family has worked this land in Quzhou for generations. My father grew wheat and corn, and so did his father. I know this soil and this weather — the flat plains, the dry springs, the rain that comes in July and August. I don't need to think hard about what to grow. The answer is the same as always: winter wheat followed by summer maize on the same land. That rotation is what works here.

I have about 10 mu of contracted land. I'll plant all 10 mu to wheat in October after the summer maize comes off. Then right after the wheat harvest in June, I'll sow maize on the same fields. One plot, two crops per year — that's how we keep income steady.

For wheat, I'll use the Jimai 22 variety that the seed shop in town sells. Everyone nearby uses it. It yields well and the millers buy it without complaint. For maize, I'll buy Xianyu 335 hybrid — it's expensive but the yield is worth it.

Fertilizer: I put down a base application of compound fertilizer before wheat planting, then top-dress urea at jointing. Same basic approach for maize — base compound, then chase it with urea at the big bell stage. I put on what my neighbor told me works and what I've seen give good results. I don't get soil tests done — they cost money and I don't fully trust them.

Water is the worry every year. We pump from the groundwater. Wheat needs water before winter sets in, again at jointing, and again at heading. Maize usually gets by with rain mostly, but if it's dry at tasseling I'll run the pump once.

I'll spray for aphids on wheat and for fall armyworm on maize. Two applications each, that's what I've always done.
